title: The Day the Sky Wore Colour — The Carrington Event of 1859
description:
On 1 September 1859 a brewer-turned-astronomer was drawing sunspots when two patches of "intensely bright and white" light appeared on the projected disc of the Sun. Seventeen and a half hours later, telegraph wires across Europe and North America began to spark, catch fire and run without batteries — while the aurora came far enough south to be seen from Havana, Honolulu, Panama and Rome.

This is the story of those five minutes and the night that followed: what Richard Carrington saw at Redhill, what the magnetometer at Kew drew in the same minute, how a billion tonnes of plasma crossed 150 million kilometres in 17.6 hours, and why the number we use for the storm's size has been argued about for a century and a half.

CHAPTERS
00:00 The sky over Rome
00:27 I — The man in the garden
01:25 II — Five minutes
02:22 III — The needle at Kew
03:23 IV — Seventeen point six hours
04:19 V — The night the sky wore colour
05:28 VI — The wires
06:55 VII — The argument about the number
08:06 VIII — The same storm, in a wired world
09:14 IX — Coda

WHAT IS SYNTHETIC, AND WHAT IS NOT
Every image in this film is drawn in code — there is no stock footage, no photographed Sun, no archival film. The Sun in this film is a simulation, not a photograph of the Sun in 1859 (no photograph of it exists). The score is synthesised. The narration is a synthetic voice (Piper, en_US-ryan-high, an open model). The Colaba and Kew magnetograms are reconstructions drawn from the published descriptions and digitised values, not scans of the original paper traces; they are labelled as reconstructions.

Every date, time, latitude, depth and nanotesla figure in the narration is taken from the peer-reviewed literature listed below. Where the literature disagrees — most importantly on the storm's intensity — the film says so instead of choosing a side.

SOURCES

The 1859 magnetograms shown are reconstructions; the Kew crochet amplitude (~−110 nT) and the Colaba excursion (~−1,600 nT) follow the published values, and the Rome observation follows Blake et al. (2020).
